guest: Compilation (Greg Newman, Tom Dante, Aaron Brown, Mike Ingram, John Moulton, Raoul Pal, Larry Hite, Rob)
style: best-of compilation: risk management
markets: oil futures, FX, bonds, ES futures, macro
edge_principles: Decide the invalidation price before entry and size so that the distance to it equals a fixed slice of capital (risk per trade = (entry - stop) / capital, Larry Hite style).
Place the stop where the thesis is wrong given normal volatility, not at an arbitrary tight distance that ordinary noise will hit.
Do not reflexively move stops to breakeven; a 'free trade' often gets scratched at support right before the intended move, and reward/risk changes as the trade progresses.
Edge = win rate x payoff; a high-win-rate style can live with ~1:1 targets, so do not distort stop/target to hit a fixed R ratio that ignores market structure.
Decide early in a trade whether it is a 'run it' trade (higher-timeframe move) or a level-to-level trade; manage accordingly.
Never average into a losing position.
Keep risk constant once a strategy is adopted instead of starting tiny and scaling up late, which leaves the largest exposure for when the edge decays.
Evaluate a model only on blocks of trades (about a month for a day trader), not after a few losses.
Risk limits should bind at survival-threatening levels; over-protection kills opportunity.
Know average win, average loss and trade frequency; changing frequency changes the risk model even with the same stop.
notes: Risk-management compilation; no concrete intraday setups, but useful sizing and breakeven-stop lessons.

style: retail FX swing/scalp, technical (fib, pivots, oscillators)
edge_principles: Focus on a single instrument until you know its 'personality', then add more.
End-of-day review ('scouting report') noting levels where price reacted and what must happen next day to continue or reverse.
Calendar all scheduled macro releases for the month in advance and plan around them.
Scaling into losers without a hard stop led to a margin call; use hard stops when away from screens and never trade on vacation from a phone/tablet.
Chasing price after alerts fire is a recurring leak.
notes: First-year retail FX trader; one loosely specified fib-confluence setup, mostly lessons about stops and preparation.

style: prop equities day trader (reversals), Kershner Trading Group
edge_principles: In a regime change, stop applying calm-market timing: panic lows arrive later/deeper, so wait for a bigger washout before buying reversals.
In high-opportunity regimes it is acceptable to take more calculated risk because recovery opportunities are abundant; in dead markets tighten risk.
Size up only when month-to-date profits give a cushion.
Manage the P&L window sorted from losers to winners: actively cut losers, leave resting exit orders on winners.
Do not anchor on 'it cannot fall further'; cut and re-enter later if the setup re-forms.
Short-sale-restriction (uptick rule after a 10% drop) changes how shorts and squeezes behave.
notes: March 2020 crisis-trading interview; reversal tactics adjusted for crash volatility, plus a capitulation-day bottom heuristic.

style: macro commentator / independent trader
edge_principles: Do not bet against an unlimited central-bank backstop; the issuer of the currency cannot run out of money.
Credit spreads (IG and high yield) and on/off-the-run spreads are the stress gauges that drive central-bank action, more than equities.
notes: Explainer on Fed QE mechanics during March 2020; macro context only, no intraday setups.

style: prop market maker in oil derivatives (Onyx Commodities)
edge_principles: When everyone is already positioned one way, very bearish news that fails to move price lower is a sign of saturation; watch the reaction to news more than the news.
Express a view in the instrument that actually reflects it (differentials/time spreads track physical reality better than the headline future).
Market makers carry residual hedged (spread/box) risk overnight, positioned for the next time zone's flow; keep outright delta near zero.
Weekend news gaps leave no chance to exit; know your weekend exposure.
notes: Oil market structure during the 2020 price war; no intraday stock setups. The 'bad news, no follow-through' idea is a general sentiment tell.

style: journalist (book on Navinder Sarao and the 2010 flash crash)
edge_principles: Sarao reportedly made most of his career profit on a small number of extreme down days; a scalper's P&L can be dominated by high-volatility sessions, so be fully engaged and sized up on those days.
Patience: watching the ladder for hours and only acting at chosen spots.
Order-book signals (large resting orders) can be fake; spoofing is illegal and not a strategy - do not rely on visible size.
notes: Story of the 'flash crash trader'; spoofing is illegal and not usable. No legitimate setups extracted.

style: ETF issuer (BetaShares)
edge_principles: Leveraged/inverse ETFs rebalance daily (or when exposure drifts out of band), so they track daily, not multi-day, index returns.
ETF price is anchored to NAV by market makers/creation-redemption; visible ETF order-book size is not informative in the way it is for stocks.
ETF fund flows (e.g. heavy buying of inverse funds) are a usable sentiment gauge.
Index rebalance trades are executed at the close on rebalance dates.
notes: ETF mechanics explainer; no setups. Possible MCF idea: inverse-ETF volume spikes as a contrarian sentiment feature.

style: prop equities day trader, SMB Capital (first full year)
markets: US stocks, high-beta names, index ETFs
edge_principles: Review stats by time of day; he lost consistently 12:00-14:00 and stopped trading then, concentrating on the first hour.
Cut everything outside your proven playbook; early losses came from feeler trades, unfamiliar symbols, thin names and repeating the same failed idea several times.
Risk a fixed fraction of the daily stop per setup type (e.g. a third for A setups, a quarter for others).
Size up mechanically: every ~10 net-green trading days, size and daily stop rise 25%.
Exit into extended, volatile candles: sell strength / cover weakness.
Use VWAP as the 'who is in control' line for in-play stocks.
A handful of outsized days a year make most of the P&L; be prepared and sized for them.
notes: SMB first-year trader; concrete pre-market-range reclaim setup and VWAP-based trend/backside trades in parabolic names.

style: HFT infrastructure (shortwave links), ex-algo trader, Bookmap origins
edge_principles: Latency-sensitive opportunities are winner-take-all; a retail/bar-based system cannot compete on speed and should avoid edges that decay in milliseconds.
Lead-lag between correlated instruments (ES leading DAX, index futures leading stocks) is the main signal HFTs pay to see first; at bar resolution such lead-lag is already arbitraged.
notes: Infrastructure/latency episode; no setups usable at MCF's 5-min resolution.

style: HFT hedge fund founder (Domeyard)
edge_principles: Short-horizon signal half-life can be 1-3 months; monitor live edge continuously and retire decayed signals without attachment.
Use a selection layer that turns signals on/off by regime rather than running everything always.
Target only a small share (about 1-3%) of a product's average daily volume to stay within capacity.
Calendar/event metadata (holidays, Fed meetings, filings) must be wired into automated strategies.
Do not overpay for marginal speed; look for lower-hanging fruit in better signals or longer holding periods.
A backtest shown once with full disclosure of methodology is more credible than a cherry-picked best run.
notes: HFT fund-building story; principles on signal decay and capacity, no setups.

guest: Compilation (Anand Sanghvi, Jared Tendler, Michael Samuels, John Moulton, Mike Bellafiore, Nishant Porbanderwalla, Jack Ma, Tom Sosnoff, Dan Shapiro)
style: best-of compilation: trading psychology
edge_principles: Asymmetric daily management (Dan Shapiro): a day that starts strongly is a 'premium hand' - do not stop at a fixed P&L goal; a day whose first trades fail within ~30 minutes should be cut off rather than pressed.
Hide the live P&L so exits follow the setup, not the dollar swing.
Never convert a short-term trade into a longer-term one because it is losing; mid-trade plan changes are usually bad.
Grade trades on process quality, not outcome; a winning trade that broke the plan is a bad trade.
Emotion accumulates across losing days ('tilt'); journal to discharge it and recognise revenge/desperation trading.
Many 'psychology' problems are really lack of edge (Bellafiore); verify the edge first.
Progress in small steps (lose less, trade flat, then small monthly targets); prop desks see substantial P&L only around year three.
Do not hold intraday positions into the close by accident; an unexecuted closing order once produced a huge overnight loss on news.
After a slump, step back and check whether the tape's behaviour has changed before re-engaging.
notes: Psychology compilation; one useful MCF-relevant rule is the day-level asymmetry (press good starts, stop after a poor start).

guest: Compilation (Lance Beggs, Ryan Trost, Tom Dante, Turney Duff, Tom Basso, James King, Charlie Bathgate, Peter Tao, Jared Tendler)
style: best-of compilation: trading psychology pt 2
edge_principles: Think about who is trapped and whose exits will push price your way (the 'meta game').
Good trading means following your strategy that day, not making money (Tom Basso via Van Tharp); change systems only outside market hours.
Over-filtering a system to remove losers tends to remove the few large winners that pay for everything.
Know the base rates of your patterns; many publicly called setups have low strike rates.
Liquidity can change structurally (e.g. OTC routing) and turn a 1x planned loss into 3x; re-check fill quality when a niche changes.
Identify your 'C-game' recurring errors; repeated errors despite more market knowledge point to an emotional cause.
Sleep and health compound into performance; small 1-2% improvements add up over a career.
notes: Psychology compilation; only Lance Beggs' weak-pullback idea is a (loose) setup.

style: fund manager, quality-growth long equities with ETF hedging
edge_principles: About 90% of institutional orders (per his broker) are VWAP algos; they slow buying when price is above VWAP and save volume for the closing auction - VWAP is a real institutional reference.
Institutions often cap participation (~10% of volume) to avoid moving price; persistent same-direction flow over days in illiquid names signals a large unfilled order.
Repeated broker 'sell lines' in a held stock are a cue to investigate fundamentals.
Cut losers and hedge quickly; a fast index-ETF hedge added large relative returns in March 2020.
Monitor positions as weights and forward upside, not as red/green P&L, to reduce emotional decisions.
Wary of mean-reversion bets on valuation gaps: someone may know why the gap exists.
notes: Institutional process and execution-algo explainer; useful for understanding intraday VWAP-driven flow.

style: quant fund (Logica Capital), long volatility / mean expansion
edge_principles: Long-volatility (calls and puts) positions bleed in quiet markets; offset the bleed by trading around the core position - trimming into short-term extensions and re-adding on dips - while keeping the convex exposure.
Overfitting happens during testing too: if a hypothesis fails, do not nudge parameters until it passes; change a parameter only with an a-priori reason, otherwise abandon the idea.
Spend more time designing the experiment than running it; expect most ideas to fail.
Run the same idea at several holding frequencies (daily, bi-weekly, monthly) so one timeframe's 'wrong' call is hedged by another.
Published white-paper factors are crowded; prefer proprietary formulations.
Passive index inflows ('if cash then buy') structurally reinforce momentum and V-shaped recoveries; use macro structure, not forecasts, to set cadence.
Media/sentiment mostly reflects the last few days' price and has little forecasting value.
notes: Volatility-strategy and research-method episode; key research-hygiene lesson on parameter tweaking; no intraday setups.

style: prop firm founder, mathematical-edge trader, ex blackjack card counter
edge_principles: Small edges (0.25-1%) become meaningful only with leverage and hedging (pairs), which makes financing costs part of the edge.
Know how brokers, clearing firms and exchanges make money (borrow fees, order flow); fees can exceed the gross edge - he once made $2.5M and paid $3M.
Hedge everything: pair a short with a related long so only the edge is exposed.
Scale the exposure of a volatility-dependent edge up and down with realised volatility.
After several losing days, cut size only if you cannot identify what changed in the market; if the edge is intact, keep size.
Look for calendar niches (Mondays, month-end) where flows repeat.
notes: Veteran's view on math edges; one concrete, testable leveraged-ETF decay trade (borrow data is the gap).

style: retail small-cap short seller (ex e-sports pro)
edge_principles: Hard daily max loss set at the broker was the single fix that stopped account blow-ups.
Systematise entry and exit triggers so they can be back-tested from saved chart screenshots and executed without hesitation.
Normalise risk in R; compound R as a % of a notional account until a target R, then 'freeze' it for 1-3 months before stepping up.
Low win rate (~26%) is fine with ~6R average winners; use small starters cut at -0.5R and add only on confirmation.
Avoid fighting hot sector momentum even in 'garbage' stocks; sector waves (e.g. cannabis) caused his big drawdown.
Do not tighten the stop just to force a 3:1 ratio; get R:R by scaling into a working trade.
Withdraw surplus profits regularly and treat trading as a paycheck rather than a high score.
Allow a number of re-entry attempts proportional to expected reward, then stop.
notes: Clear small-cap backside short framework with R-based risk model and explicit stats.

style: prop equities (Seven Points Capital), discretionary momentum and small-cap shorts
edge_principles: Beginners should learn trend-joining pullbacks rather than reversal picks; better reward/risk and easier execution.
Squeeze warning signs for shorts: breakdowns that do not follow through, new highs after 10:30-11:00 in a low float, and volume far above the float without price falling.
Daily lockout = average green day over the last 21 days, so a max-loss day only gives back about one good day; unlock only if not on tilt.
On a losing streak halve daily risk, and halve again, until green days return; then size back up.
Write a per-setup list of allowed exit reasons and grade exits against it.
Need 30-40+ trades per setup before judging it; track stats by setup (separate accounts help).
New strategies go to a 'lab' at small size and graduate to more capital only when they work.
In quiet markets do less; do not use experiments as an excuse to be busy.
Only winning day trades may become overnight holds.
notes: Listener Q&A with a prop firm partner; several small-cap short patterns and strong risk-control rules.

style: activist short seller (Wolfpack Research)
markets: US-listed stocks incl. China reverse mergers
edge_principles: Red flags for fundamental shorts: margins far above peers, sudden last-minute rescues, executive history, heavy reliance on 'adjusted' metrics tied to management bonuses, debt-funded roll-ups that overpay.
Verify claims through customers, suppliers, ex-employees and physical observation rather than management.
Even a correct thesis can be squeezed by a promotional press release; size short positions so a 100% move is survivable and keep a 'squeal point'.
Build positions at no more than ~5-10% of daily volume to avoid alerting the market.
notes: Activist-short research process; fundamental/forensic, no intraday setups. Shows that sudden PR can double a heavily shorted fraud.

style: quant fund-of-funds allocator (T2AM)
edge_principles: Alpha comes from identifiable inefficiencies or indifference of other participants (e.g. sloppy institutional execution, passive index funds); when the cause changes, the old model stops working.
A large share of US equity volume now trades at the close (market-on-close), which matters for intraday strategy design.
Any mean-reversion model must account for index rebalance flows to avoid fading forced buying/selling.
Narrow (sector/company-specific) models and alternative data trade more fitting risk for stronger priors; out-of-sample R^2 of ~0.03 is a success in markets.
Individual quants are better off licensing signals than starting a fund.
notes: Trends in quant investing; one concrete index-reconstitution idea, plus a useful flag to avoid fading index flows.

style: ex-prop futures trader, own fund (Habitus Capital), human + automation hybrid
edge_principles: Separate 'context filters' (which market, what regime) from 'signals' (when a strategy is valid); a strategy is only an opportunity inside the right context.
Predefine every controllable decision (entry, stop, target, size, expected behaviour) on a per-strategy cue card; no thinking while risk is on.
Log what the system said vs what you did each day and review the deviations (he deviates 5-6 times a day) to improve both trader and system.
Edge lies in how a strategy is applied (filters, validity checks, sizing), not in the pattern itself.
Set your own rules for engagement (e.g. only trade first and last hour) to narrow focus.
Use a systematic risk tool that computes size from stop distance and flags under/over-risking.
Watch positioning: crowded positioning reduces asymmetry; enter when crowd is neutral or after a counter-move.
Avoid narrative bias against markets you do not understand; go where volatility and opportunity are.
notes: Process-focused futures trader; breakout setup with explicit post-entry validity checks that MCF could encode as early exits.

style: independent equity research / fundamental investor (Veritas, Antya)
markets: large-cap North American and Indian equities
edge_principles: Read five years of reports to judge consistency of disclosure; one year hides the trend.
Accounting can be technically allowed yet make no business sense (capitalised maintenance, intra-group asset sales booked as gains, re-labelled defaulted loans).
Use physical/alternative counts (e.g. directory pages and ads across cities) to see revenue decline hidden by price rises and acquisitions.
Large caps re-price to fundamentals quickly once institutions exit; markets can stay irrational longer than you stay solvent.
notes: Fundamental research case studies (Kingfisher, Reliance Communications, BlackBerry, Yellow Pages, Tesla); no trading setups.

style: prop equities (SMB/KTG), intraday momentum with selective swings
markets: US stocks: low floats, OTC, large caps
edge_principles: Spend the first months trading everything at tiny size, logging all trades, then keep only the segment where data shows edge (for him: shorting low floats).
Think of risk per trade as a fixed % of the daily stop so size-ups keep the same proportions; hide live P&L.
Allocate ~10% of the daily stop per intraday name, but 50-100% on rare A+ swings with 5-10:1 reward/risk.
Fund overnight short risk with that day's realised profit in the same name; never open a fresh overnight low-float short right before the close.
Three strikes rule: after three failed trades in one stock, stop trading it that day.
Rules on screen: do not short a stock trending above VWAP, do not buy one trending below, do not trade a range.
'Change of character' (losing VWAP, high-volume topping bar then lower high) is the exit signal.
Pre-write staged profit targets for swings to stop scalping out early; use a hotkey that scales out tiny pieces to satisfy the urge.
Set alarms every 30 minutes to zoom out to higher timeframes.
notes: Strong low-float short and theme-sympathy swing frameworks with concrete management rules.

style: prop equities (Seven Points Capital), intraday short bias + swing long breakouts + options wheel
edge_principles: Daily lockout = 2x median green day over the last ~22 trading days; risk per trade = 1/6 to 1/8 of the lockout (max 1/4 on the best setups). Size then grows automatically with performance.
Using median rather than mean green day removes outlier days from the sizing base.
Oversizing one trade caused his worst loss and led him to dump a winning swing position; follow the sizing plan.
Watch a basket of 10-15 related high-beta names to read relative strength/weakness and lead-lag.
Only add to shorts on red candles after a lower high, never into a green candle.
Tape/L2 is now full of spoofing; a 1-second chart conveys the same information with less noise.
Avoid dilutive small caps for long swings.
Options: sell far OTM cash-secured puts on quality stocks when implied volatility is high (after 3-4 red days or around earnings), buy back at ~90% of premium.
notes: Clear, codeable sizing model and three concrete setups (swing breakout, recycled trend short, washout flip).

style: independent momentum swing trader (ex day trader)
edge_principles: Build a large screenshot database of every historical instance of your setup (before/after, daily and intraday) to learn its variations; patterns repeat over 100 years.
Breakouts work in up/sideways markets and mostly fail in falling markets; the best entries come right after a market correction in stocks that held up best.
Trailing MA exits should be on a closing basis; intraday undercuts are common noise.
Overriding his own sell rules (selling 'overextended' winners early) costs him money about three quarters of the time.
Scale risk with account size in percentage terms; use margin only when performance has earned it, cut exposure in corrections.
Having ~30 open positions has coincided with market tops (crowded exposure as a contrarian signal).
Fewer indicators; focus on price and ignore media opinion.
Know the fundamental or thematic 'fuel'; it adds conviction and holding power.
notes: Very concrete swing breakout method with explicit entry (opening-range high), stop (day low) and trailing exits - highly codeable for MCF daily+intraday data.

style: prop (KTG), evolved from click trader to automated portfolio with ML scoring
edge_principles: Mine your own journal for the one thing that consistently works and do only that ('pile of money in the corner'); his first edge was a now-dead NYSE Arca ETF closing-auction quirk.
Edges decay within months; keep building a portfolio of strategies (mean reversion, momentum, news/earnings keyword, seasonal analyst-rating cycles, M&A season).

Anything that can hurt P&L (risk limits, kill switches) must be under your own control and independently redundant; a buggy stop-loss once flipped a 25k-share position back and forth for 7 seconds and nearly zeroed the account.
Use truly out-of-sample evaluation; simple OLS was his best model, XGBoost as a second opinion for tail risk, k-means to split regimes/clusters.
Models that can only veto trades may be opaque; models that can say 'yes' must be fully understood.
Think small: compound a tiny edge, e.g. raise size ~1% per day while it keeps working.
Strategies like meme-stock trades are cyclical between momentum and mean-reversion phases; identify the phase.
notes: Automation/ML-focused prop trader; strong risk-engineering lessons; setups mostly order-book or historical.

style: performance coach (ex commodity-firm performance director)
edge_principles: Find where most results come from (Pareto, like tennis serve/return winning ~85% of points) and put most effort there; most top traders win by mastering basics and avoiding big errors.
Train on the specific situations that break down live, under realistic stress, with variability rather than rote repetition.
Under pressure, shrink the problem: fewer positions, smaller size, more time.
Guard against continuity bias and the illusion of control after success; assume conditions will change.
Improve via small experiments with a plan; failure is data.
Pick the trading style, asset class and firm that fit your strengths, interests and values.
notes: Elite-performance framework; no setups.

style: quant sports-betting trading firm founder (Seamless Capital), ex poker pro
markets: sports betting exchanges (Hong Kong horse racing, football, tennis)
edge_principles: Repeated blow-ups came from scaling stakes/size faster than edge and bankroll allowed; size relative to bankroll (Kelly-style) and stop after a fixed % loss when outclassed.
Pair an optimistic idea generator with a pessimistic risk reviewer; debating every scale-up stopped the blow-ups.
Large positions are accumulated in small clips, waiting for liquidity to refresh, to avoid scaring the other side.
Simple filters can add a lot: e.g. stop trading long shots where a model over-weights them.
Small traders should pick markets too small for institutions; large teams go where liquidity is.
Spend ~20% of time on 'wildcard' ideas; most fail but a few are gems.
Borrow techniques from other fields (e.g. ML methods from image recognition).
notes: Sports-betting quant story; no market setups, but useful sizing and team-risk lessons.

style: billionaire investor / entrepreneur (Burnbrae Group)
markets: emerging markets, real estate, biotech, private companies
edge_principles: Avoid concentration and leverage: a 1998 Russia default cost half a year's profit in days and triggered a large margin call; he now runs core assets with no debt.
Specialise first, diversify only once capital allows.
Entry price matters even for great businesses; weigh management quality and plan against valuation.
Calm in crashes comes from experience that markets recover; in frothy markets shift focus to protecting downside.
notes: Long-horizon investor biography; no trading setups.

style: mental game coach (author, Mental Game of Trading)
edge_principles: Map each recurring error with its triggers on a 1-10 intensity scale and find the tipping point to intervene before control is lost.
Grade each day as A/B/C game independent of P&L, since short-term P&L gives false feedback.
Start-of-day C-game: trade smaller or warm up first.
For regime changes that kill a playbook: decide early in the day if conditions fit; otherwise stop trading or treat it as small-size research.
Use a 20-trade execution-only checklist block to decouple from P&L.
Most 'greed' and 'hesitation' are symptoms of fear, anger or confidence flaws (e.g. belief that a missed trade can be made up).
notes: Psychology method; no setups. The 'decide early whether today's regime suits the playbook' rule maps to an MCF regime gate.

style: ASX small-cap trader, placements specialist (180 Markets)
edge_principles: Make hay in good patches; in bad patches cut size to about 20% rather than stop entirely.
Runs of wins and runs of losses both trigger a 'gambler mentality' of oversizing; after either, take a zero off size.
Treat displayed big bids with suspicion; they are often not real.
Liquidity first: only size up where you can exit; exit large positions into high-volume events rather than into thin markets.
Placements: oversubscribed raises with reputable brokers tend to trade well afterwards; weak ones fall back to the placement price; companies raise after price rises.
Avoid stocks where a director's advisory firm takes fees on raisings.
notes: ASX small-cap and capital-raising perspective; one loose sector-laggard swing setup.

style: short-focused research newsletter writer (The Bear Cave)
edge_principles: Red flags: frequent CFO/board/auditor turnover (esp. exits within months), executives whose prior companies collapsed, buzzword-heavy CEO talk, many consumer complaints, SEC comment letters (CORRESP) questioning metrics.
Misconduct concentrates in sub-$1-5B market caps with little institutional scrutiny.
Short-only portfolios fight ~9%/yr market drift and crowded, expensive borrows; keep shorts small.
Activist reports covered on the publication day signal a dishonest actor; short-report pops reflect that.
Short interest above 100% of float is mechanically normal (re-lent shares), not proof of manipulation.
notes: Fundamental short-research process; no trading setups.

style: options market maker CEO (Simplex Trading)
edge_principles: Market makers assume prevailing prices are mostly right; edge = deviation from a fair value (~mid) minus fees, required per trade and recalibrated from realised slippage data.
Heavy one-sided call buying forces dealers short gamma; their delta hedging (buying stock into rallies) can amplify squeezes - relevant to meme/high call-volume names.
Self-calibrating systems adjust to volatility automatically; parameters change only on data-backed cases, weekly or slower.
Retail options volume in 2021 stayed extremely elevated even with low realised volatility.
Hiring/skills: data handling and quantitative case-making matter more than finance background.
notes: Options market-making explainer; no directional setups. Gamma-squeeze mechanics useful context for momentum names with heavy call volume.

style: crypto hedge fund CIO (Astronaut Capital), ex FX/commodities trader
edge_principles: Assume black-swan moves (30-50% in minutes) can happen; never rely on distant liquidation levels with leverage - a single-venue flash crash liquidated his position before price recovered.
Excess leverage (3-4x) is what killed crypto funds in big drawdowns.
Relative strength on down/flat market days is an early signal of a rotating theme.
Pairs (long strong theme name / short a name expected to get hit) reduce shock risk.
Going fully flat when market structure turns bearish is acceptable; re-enter higher quickly if wrong.
Benchmark performance against simply holding the main asset.
Size so you can sleep; prefer large liquid assets as a newcomer.
notes: Crypto fund manager; thematic-rotation breakout idea transferable to stock sectors.

style: M&A/takeover arbitrage hedge fund CIO (Harvest Lane)
edge_principles: Size event trades by worst-case downside: shares = risk dollars / (entry - estimated deal-break price).
Diversify across many deals driven by independent factors; M&A returns are largely uncorrelated to the market.
A widening spread over time signals waning confidence; normally the spread should narrow toward completion.
Opening prints above a conditional bid often reflect short covering after the announcement; check short interest before chasing.
Read deal documents for the unusual clause (e.g. go-shop); value is in what differs from boilerplate.
Cap upside chasing: trim when price is >10% above the best bid.
notes: Detailed merger-arb process; event-driven swing setup needing an M&A dataset.

guest: Compilation (Michael Katz, Alex 'Tagger', Liam Vaughan, Nishant Porbanderwalla, Brian Lee, Dennis Dick, Phil Goedeker, Jeff Davis)
style: best-of compilation: day trading pt 1
edge_principles: Katz/Porbanderwalla/Lee clips repeat setups already extracted in ep205/ep191/ep204.
The open is where HFT market makers withdraw; price discovery creates the most dislocation and opportunity (Dennis Dick).
Trade market-neutral by hedging net beta exposure with SPY when holding many opening fills.
Know which regime your setups work in; when one setup family starts losing after a strong run, expect a regime change and reduce size rather than try to call the turn (Jeff Davis).
Index futures trend intraday only ~15% of the time; 'the trend is your friend' does not hold at short horizons.
Specialise in one product or niche to reach confidence and size.
Short sellers of low floats use multiple brokers for locates and fee differences; locate/borrow fees can take 10-15%+ of profits (Goedeker).
Increase size on 'golden' setups only gradually (10-15%, then 25-50%).
notes: Compilation with two strong codeable ideas: opening-auction fair-value fade and ATR-gated mean reversion.

guest: Compilation (Stan Gluzman, Sam Bankman-Fried, Peter Tao, Christina Qi, Ryan Hasson, Nick Fabbrio, John Roberson, Nico, Tom Dante)
style: best-of compilation: day trading pt 2
edge_principles: Gluzman/Hasson/Roberson/Qi clips repeat material already extracted in ep211/ep210/ep213/ep198.
Dark-pool/aggregator pinging can reveal whether a real buyer is behind a rise; when the buyer disappears, flip (Gluzman, needs routing access).
Arbitrage and liquidity provision are the same act: sell where customers are buying, buy where they are selling (SBF).
Conventional rules (never average down, never fade trends) are violated by some successful traders; find the process that fits you (Peter Tao).
Bearish technicals plus bearish consensus that fail to produce a breakdown are a long signal (Tom Dante).
Fast reaction to price-sensitive news (e.g. guidance reaffirmed after repeated downgrades) can be a short-term edge on ASX (Nick Fabbrio).
Being early costs small paper cuts that prevent full size at the real turn (Nico).
notes: Compilation; new concrete ideas are Tom Dante's gap-failure fade and resistance-probe, plus Nico's patient stop-entry reversal.

style: systematic futures CTA (Ravinia Investment Management)
markets: equity index, treasury and currency futures
edge_principles: Build a portfolio by exposure type: intraday momentum (long-vol, crisis alpha), mean reversion (incl. open mean reversion), mid-frequency swing; diversify across style, holding period and trade structure (high win-rate vs low win-rate).
Check correlations during crisis periods, not just full-sample averages.
Limit optimised parameters to 2-4; use cluster walk-forward (vary IS/OOS split and window) and check that small parameter changes do not collapse results.
Back-test over the longest history to include many volatility events; inspect each drawdown to understand when the strategy should fail.
Optimise for return/max-drawdown (Calmar); a Calmar of 2-3 is strong and leverage then sets the return/drawdown level.
Trailing stops on daily bars can inflate back-tests due to intrabar path assumptions; use fixed stops/targets or intrabar simulation.
Intervene only to reduce risk, never to predict.
notes: Systematic CTA; gap-momentum/ORB core with robust-testing guidance directly relevant to MCF lab methodology.

style: ASX small-cap swing trader (trade recap)
edge_principles: Anchor stops and size to a fundamental floor (cash backing) and to order-book liquidity in thin stocks.
Go hard on the one or two A+ setups per year that meet every criterion.
Use catalyst days as exit liquidity; heavy books on 'good news' signal sell-the-news.
Known weakness: selling too early ahead of blow-off moves (the last 2-3 days often deliver as much as the prior month).
notes: Trade recap; catalyst-driven small-cap base trade.

style: prop day trader (Trillium), capitulation/exhaustion specialist
edge_principles: Capitulation = rapid exponential price change plus extreme volume turnover; trade it reactively.
The more boring and liquid the instrument, the more reliable the overshoot reversal.
Measure value against where price spent long periods in equilibrium; buy at a discount.
Risk is often lowest at peak panic, provided the trade is structured safely.
Learn the easiest, most repeatable plays first; deliberate practice and reviewing a database of 40-50 past plays weekly.
Set a time stop on a trading career and persist through a slow start.
notes: Part 1 of 2; career story, learning methods, capitulation framework.

style: prop day trader (Trillium), part 2
edge_principles: Deliberate practice: reflect on every rep and keep a database of past great plays to rehearse.
Reverse-engineer surprising reactions to news, e.g. a stock rising on bad-but-feared news as a 'clearing event'; trend with it once it starts to move.
Markets keep getting more efficient, so you must improve each year just to hold P&L steady.
Each day, find the easiest change with the largest impact (e.g. stop trading after-hours earnings where you have no edge).
Judge days by whether you improved, not by P&L colour; do a daily review.
Remove execution friction: hotkeys rather than the mouse, and automate routines.
notes: Mostly process, technology and philanthropy; the clearing-event idea is too vague to record as a setup.

style: crypto market maker / arbitrage fund (Proxima Capital)
edge_principles: Arbitrage and market making both come down to estimating a fair global price from many order books and only trading at better than fair.
Get spot execution efficient first; every derivative and hedged strategy depends on cheap risk lay-off.
Structural edges (leverage demand, scarce credit) are time-limited; expect P&L to decay and keep innovating.
Avoid markets whose reference index you cannot arbitrage yourself.
Scale through engineering breadth (many venues and pairs) rather than star traders.
notes: Crypto only; the basis trade cannot be tested with MCF data. Early part covers the founder's mining and DEX background.

style: niche equities trader: ADRs/dual listings, index rebalances, crypto lead-lag
edge_principles: Compete where others can't or won't; niches have less competition.
Edge sources: Access, Speed, Information, Analytics; pre-game events so you act while others are still asking questions.
Size exponentially, not linearly, for A+ trades; be a pig when confidence is truly high.
Be wary of getting big volume at great prices; check for raisings/takeovers first (learned through costly losses).
Test 'common sense' relationships (e.g. gold vs gold miners via hedging and FX); many don't hold.
Edges decay as they get crowded (index rebalances; an ETH lag behind Nasdaq shrank from minutes to seconds).
Playbook everything, then backtest recurring oddities.
notes: Strong source of structural/event edges; the overnight-hold idea is directly testable in MCF.

style: prop day trader, trade recap (DWAC Oct 2021)
edge_principles: Drop valuation bias; a day trader trades the next 10-20 minutes, not the story.
Once the main move (squeeze and first flush) is done, the edge is gone; risk at most ~10% of the day's P&L poking around.
Size to what you can exit if the thesis vanishes (imbalance disappears).
Use pre-set hotkeys (marketable limit 'delta' orders) to exit instantly when wrong.
Understand market microstructure (opening imbalances, LULD bands, halt reopen auctions) as an edge.
notes: Trade recap; day 1 lost about $23k fighting the trend from bias, day 2 was a large winner.

style: SMB Capital prop trader, multi-strategy, short bias
markets: US equities, options (as a hedge), index scalping when volatile
edge_principles: Trade tiny (100-share lots, tiny daily stop) until consistency is proven; never dig a hole.
Set process goals (one focus per day, three or four per month), grade daily, review monthly.
Grow the daily stop gradually (e.g. +10-15%) after record months and keep per-trade risk at ~10% of the daily stop.
When in doubt, get out; never add to a squeezing loser.
Lower stress points: hedge front-side trades with options; carry only winners or hedged positions overnight.
Keep adding strategies with small size and rotate toward what the current market rewards; avoid complacency.
Breadth: more good bets means more consistency.
notes: Mostly development and mindset; setups are lightly specified.
